tools: CART trees: greedy binary splits scored by Gini, entropy (log_loss) or squared error; knobs max_depth, min_samples_leaf, ccp_alpha.
Readable rules, quick explainers, leakage checks; the building block of forests and boosting.
Print or draw a fitted tree's questions and leaf predictions.
Explaining a small tree to people; checking that the first split makes sense.
Lists the ccp_alpha values at which branches of a fully grown tree get pruned away.
Many deep trees on bootstrap samples with a random subset of features per split (max_features, default "sqrt" for classifiers, 1.0 for regressors); oob_score=True for a free estimate.
The strong first model for a tabular problem; near-zero tuning; robust to noise.
Extremely randomized trees: random thresholds as well as random features; no bootstrap by default.
Even lower variance and faster training than a random forest; sometimes a little more accurate.
Train any model on bootstrap samples and average or vote; default base model is a decision tree; supports oob_score.
Reducing the variance of an unstable model; comparing plain bagging with a random forest.
AdaBoost: decision stumps trained in sequence on re-weighted data; each gets a vote α = ½ ln((1 − err)/err).
Teaching boosting; simple problems with clean labels.

Classic gradient boosting (Friedman): each small tree fits the negative gradient; learning_rate, n_estimators, subsample; early stopping with n_iter_no_change + validation_fraction; staged_predict for per-round curves.
Small data (under ~10,000 rows), teaching, per-round analysis.
LightGBM-inspired boosting: ≤ 255 histogram bins, native NaN handling, categorical_features="from_dtype", max_leaf_nodes=31, early stopping automatic above 10,000 rows.
The default boosted-tree model when you want no extra dependency.

Regularized gradient boosting with second-order (Newton) steps, learned default directions for missing values, tree_method="hist" (default), device="cuda", early_stopping_rounds in the constructor, enable_categorical=True.
Large tabular problems, GPUs, Spark/Dask, competitions; version 3.4 as of late 2026.
Histogram boosting with leaf-wise growth (num_leaves, default 31), GOSS (data_sample_strategy="goss"), EFB, native categoricals; early stopping via the lgb.early_stopping callback.
Very large or wide/sparse data where training speed matters; version 4.7 as of late 2026.
Boosting with ordered target statistics for categorical features (cat_features), optional ordered boosting (boosting_type="Ordered"), symmetric trees (grow_policy="SymmetricTree", depth=6).
Many or high-cardinality categoricals; strong defaults with little tuning; fast inference; version 1.2 as of late 2026.
Fits a meta-model (final_estimator) on out-of-fold predictions of the base models (cv=5 by default); passthrough adds the original features.
Combining diverse models when a small accuracy gain is worth extra complexity.
Combines models with fixed (optionally weighted) votes: voting="hard" on labels or "soft" on probabilities.
A quick, safe ensemble of a few good, different models.
Returns, for every row, the prediction of a model trained on the other folds: out-of-fold predictions.
Building stacking/blending features without leakage; honest residual plots.
AutoML that trains many model families and combines them with multi-layer stacking, from one line of Python.
Strong tabular baselines and competitions when compute is available.
auto-sklearn, H2O AutoML, a single GBDT

A transformer pre-trained on millions of synthetic datasets that predicts a new table in one forward pass (in-context learning); Nature 2025 version evaluated up to 10,000 rows and 500 features; newer versions list larger limits; weights under non-commercial licences.
Small tables where accuracy matters and inference latency doesn't; compare with a GBDT on the same folds.
acronyms: Breiman et al.'s 1984 tree algorithm: binary splits, Gini or squared error, cost-complexity pruning. scikit-learn's trees are an optimized CART.
Quinlan's tree learners that choose splits by information gain (entropy); C4.5 added numeric thresholds, missing values and pruning.
The roughly 37% of training rows a bootstrap sample leaves out; predicting them gives a free validation estimate.
gradient boosting machine / gradient-boosted decision trees
An additive model of small trees, each fitted to the negative gradient (residuals) of the loss of the trees before it.
LightGBM's sampling: keep the rows with the largest gradients, sample the rest, and up-weight the sampled ones by (1 − a)/b.
LightGBM packs sparse columns that are rarely non-zero at the same time into one column, so there are fewer columns to scan.
wide, sparse data such as one-hot features
Encoding a category by (a smoothed) average of the target over its rows; CatBoost computes them in an ordered way to avoid leaks.
A tabular foundation model: a transformer trained on synthetic datasets that learns a new table in context.
A standard fully connected neural network; rotation-invariant and sensitive to useless features on tables.
terms: A model that asks a sequence of yes/no questions about single features and predicts the majority label (or average value) of the training rows in the final box.
A final box of a tree; it predicts the majority class or the average target of the training rows that land in it.
How mixed the labels in a node are: 0 when pure. Gini, entropy and variance are the common measures.
1 − Σ p²: the chance two random members of a node have different labels. 0.5 for a 50/50 node.
−Σ p log₂ p: average bits of surprise per member of a node; 1 bit for 50/50.
The drop in entropy from a parent node to its size-weighted children; the split score in ID3/C4.5.
Parent impurity minus the size-weighted impurity of the children; the tree picks the split with the largest gain.
Choosing the best split for the current node only, never looking ahead; fast, but can miss XOR-like patterns where the first split looks useless.
Stopping a tree early (max_depth, min_samples_leaf) vs growing it fully and then cutting back weak branches (ccp_alpha).
Post-pruning that minimizes total leaf impurity + α × number of leaves: every leaf has a price α.
A tree for numeric targets: splits reduce variance and each leaf predicts the mean, so the prediction is a step function.
Predicting outside the range seen in training; tree models are flat beyond the last threshold, so they can't continue trends.
n rows drawn with replacement from n; some rows repeat, about 37% are left out.
Bootstrap aggregating: train models on bootstrap samples and average or vote; reduces variance.
Bagged deep trees that also pick a random subset of features at every split, so the trees are less correlated.
How many randomly chosen features each split may consider; smaller means less correlated but weaker trees.
Trees that pick split thresholds at random as well as features, for even more decorrelation.
How alike the errors of different trees are; the variance of an average of B trees is ρσ² + (1 − ρ)σ²/B, so ρ sets a floor.
A tree with a single split.
A model only slightly better than guessing; boosting combines many into a strong one.
Training models in sequence, each focusing on what the ensemble so far gets wrong, and adding them up; reduces bias.
Boosting by re-weighting: misclassified points get heavier; each stump votes with weight α = ½ ln((1 − err)/err).
Each new tree fits the negative gradient of the loss (the residuals for squared error) and is added with a learning rate.
Target minus prediction, y − ŷ: what the model still gets wrong; the next tree's training target in gradient boosting with squared error.
The factor η by which each new tree's prediction is scaled before being added; smaller needs more rounds but is more forgiving.
Watching validation loss after every round and stopping when it hasn't improved for a set number of rounds (patience), keeping the best round.
Each tree is fitted on a random subsample of rows (subsample < 1); faster and slightly regularizing.
The curvature of the loss at a prediction; XGBoost uses it for Newton steps: leaf value −G/(H + λ).
XGBoost's tree objective: loss + γ per leaf + ½λ Σ w²; γ refuses weak splits, λ shrinks small leaves.
At each split, learning the best default direction for rows with missing (or zero) values and scanning only the present ones.
XGBoost's way of proposing split candidates at quantiles of each feature, weighted by the hessian.
Pre-cutting each feature into at most ~255 bins so a split search scans bin totals instead of every value.
Splitting all leaves of one depth before going deeper vs always splitting the single leaf with the biggest gain (lower loss for the same leaves, but can overfit small data).
Encoding each row's category with the target average of only the rows before it in a random order, so no row sees its own label.
CatBoost's fix for the small target leak in standard boosting, where each tree's residuals are computed on the same rows it was fitted to.
A tree that uses the same split at every node of a level; a depth-d tree is d yes/no answers indexing 2^d leaves; fast to evaluate.
Combining several models' predictions with weights (or a meta-model) fitted on a held-out set.
Training a meta-model on base models' out-of-fold predictions so it learns how to combine them (Wolpert 1992, Breiman 1996).
The second-level model in stacking; usually simple (linear or logistic regression).
Predictions for each row from a model trained on the other folds; the leak-free input for stacking and target encoding.
How much two models' errors move together; the lower it is, the more a blend can gain.
The assumptions a model family makes about what functions are likely (trees: axis-aligned steps; NNs: smooth functions).
A learner whose results don't change if the feature space is rotated (k-NN with Euclidean distance, standard MLPs); a weakness on tables, where columns have meaning.
A column that carries no information about the target; trees ignore it, distance-based models and MLPs get diluted by it.
A model pre-trained across many (often synthetic) tables that predicts a new table without task-specific training, e.g. TabPFN.
Learning a task from examples given in the input at prediction time, with no weight updates; how TabPFN “fits” a table.
